newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Mrs. Clinton begins four-day trip to Tanzania.
newsitem.headline: Mrs. Clinton begins four-day trip to Tanzania.

text.p: Tanzanian women wrapped a traditional Khanga garment around U.S. First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton on Monday then clapped their hands and cheered to welcome her on a four-day visit to this East African nation.

In a prelude to a visit to Tanzania's northern safari country -- the exotic high point of her two-week tour of Africa -- Mrs. Clinton and her daughter Chelsea flew from Zimbabwe to the Tanzanian capital, Dar es Salaam, situated on the Indian Ocean.

President Clinton's wife paid a courtesy call on President Benjamin Mkapa, held a roundtable discussion with Tanzanian women on their work to improve their status in the male- dominated society, saw a skull touted as the world's oldest and praised Tanzania's humanitarian role in easing Africa's refugee crisis.

After an hour-long discussion with the women, interrupted once by the screeching of a peacock perched atop the National Museum building where the roundtable was held, a Tanzanian women's rights advocate, Gertrude Mongello, presented Mrs. Clinton with a Khanga.

It is a traditional garment used for just about everything -- a dress, a skirt, a shawl, even a tablecloth. The inscription on Mrs. Clinton's said: "The value of a mother increases. It is like precious gold."
She wrapped it around like a dress on the clearly delighted Mrs. Clinton, who insisted she keep it on when the women tried to take it off. "Leave it on," she said.
The women clapped their hands and gave ululations of joy as they escorted Mrs. Clinton out of the humid room.

During the session, Mrs. Clinton praised Tanzania for providing refugees with a safe haven from crises in Burundi and Zaire. U.S. officials estimate at least 300,000 refugees from Burundi and Zaire are on Tanzanian soil.

"The United States is certainly aware of the unique role that Tanzania has played in keeping the peace and being gracious and hospitable to the refugees that come across your border seeking safety. It is an enormous burden that you have borne," Mrs. Clinton said.
She also urged Tanzania to stay on the path of economic reform and cultural transformation even when times are rough.
"It will not be without difficulties here in this country," she said. "Take on these hard issues now. They will not be any easier if they are postponed. They will only become more difficult."
Tanzanian women told Mrs. Clinton they were seeking to improve their education and training, gain legal rights, reduce sexual violence, and cut AIDS infections.
Zakia Meghji, Tanzanian minister of natural resources, said more women need to be involved in policy-making decisions in government.
"If we have more women in policy-making positions, changes will take place," she said.

Mrs. Clinton crossed to another museum building and took a look at an Australopithecus skull called the world's oldest at 1.75 million years old. Mary Leakey found it in 1959 in Tanzania's Olduvai Gorge, which Mrs. Clinton will visit later this week along with the Ngorongoro Crater and the Serengeti Plain.
Mrs. Clinton told reporters she hopes her trip, which ends March 30, will call attention to Africans' work to strengthen their economies and build their democracies.

"If my coming here can bring more attention to this continent and particularly to the countries we visit, I hope that that will help Americans to have a broader understanding of Africa, and understand more fully the real stake we have in a successful, prosperous, stable Africa in the future," she said.
